mortality rates of infectious diseases.  Our analysis using data on 135 diseases
from 57 low- and middle-income countries between 2009 and 2019 reveals that the
mortality rates we estimated are generally consistent with existing research, yet
the analysis of incidence data proves more complicated due to varying data
quality, resulting in less reliable estimates.  Focusing on 41 diseases with well-
qualited incidence data, our results indicate a substantial proportion exhibit
peaks in age-specific incidence and mortality rates, often found at middle age.
Diseases with higher transmission risks tend to show different patterns in incidence
and mortality rates, whereas those with lower transmission risks exhibit similar
patterns in incidence and mortality rates, all of which peak at the same age.
Notably, mortality rates are significantly influenced by age-specific incidence
rates, as well as peaks in the two rates occurring at the same age; however, the
shape of the mortality rate curve cannot be accurately predicted solely from
the incidence rate curve.  Our research highlights the significance of collecting
incidence data and engaging in comparative epidemiological research when evaluating
intervention strategies and developing control measures for infectious diseases. 
Our findings also suggest modeling mortality rates directly may not adequately
capture the intricate dynamics of disease spread, thereby underestimating the
complexity of age-specific mortality rate analysis.  Furthermore, our study shows
results that raise important questions about public health data, research methods,
and the interpretation of results, highlighting potential areas for future
investigation, including modeling incidence and mortality rates simultaneously,
as well as exploring disease prevalence across different age groups.

creating indoor maps through map-building techniques is a crucial task.  Utilizing Wi-Fi signal strength, a popular method for localization, leverages a database of previously measured signal strengths against map coordinates.  However, constructing such a large database of reference Wi-Fi signal strengths across an entire map is a significant challenge, leading researchers to explore alternative approaches that rely solely on real-time Wi-Fi measurements during the map-building process.  Existing studies often focus on constructing databases for specific areas, failing to address the broader issue of developing a method that adapts to new environments.  In response, we've developed a method for online indoor map-building, demonstrating its effectiveness in adaptability by applying it to multiple diverse locations.  Comparing our method's accuracy to other approaches, we've found it excels in areas with low mobility.  We've gathered data sets for seven different environments as an open-source contribution, making our method publicly available online.  In testing this method, we used a multi-KNearest Neighbor approach that combines signal strength readings from multiple query points, calculating the distance between a measurement point and the map grid cells.  With a 1 centimeter grid size, a mobility rate of 10 percent, and 20 query points per floor, our method achieves a root mean square error of 1.5 meters when building maps during the map-building process.  We've demonstrated that reducing the grid size or increasing the mobility rate results in decreased accuracy, notability exceeding 20 percent mobility rate.  We've gathered 49 megabyte data sets for seven diverse locations as a supplementary file, including map visualizations.  Our method's source code is available for public access.

shift bins in large galaxy surveys like the Dark Energy Survey (DES) and Euclid. These surveys divide the cosmos into distinct redshift ranges to study how galaxies and cosmological phenomena evolve over time. Our study focuses on the statistical variations of these bins due to the sampling of a vast universe containing many independent galaxy populations. These variations affect researchers' ability to track the evolution of galaxies and cosmological phenomena. Our findings are based on a simplified representation of the universe, where we simulate galaxy surveys using overdensities and field distributions. These simulations allow us to understand the variations within each bin due to the sampling of multiple independent regions of the universe. As a result, we can determine the precision with which researchers can measure the galaxy distribution within each bin. These precision values are a function of the number of galaxies in each bin, the density of galaxies, and any density of cosmic overdensities that the survey is sensitive to. These precision values have implications for how researchers should select the width of their redshift bins to accurately measure the evolution of galaxies and cosmological phenomena. For example, in the DES, the ideal bin width is around 0.05 in z-space, but it can be broader for the Euclid. These findings can also reduce the sample variance when modeling the galaxy distribution within these redshift bins. These reductions can be used to improve the accuracy of theoretical models in predicting how the galaxy distribution changes over time with increasing redshift. This, in turn, can help streamline the process of conducting a DES-Euclid cross-correlation and creating a more accurate reconstruction of the galaxy distribution across wide spatial areas. 

  Our study shows that the variations within these bins due to large-scale structure should not be overlooked as they can affect research seeking to track the evolution of galaxies and cosmological phenomena. By estimating these fluctuations using survey properties, we can set a handle on how precise the evolutionary parameters can be measured. This is demonstrated in an analysis of a simplified galaxy survey represented by a cosmic overdensity. 

  We have developed an appraised Precision Calculator that can estimate these fluctuations for any survey based on its characteristics and those of a specific cosmic population being tracked. This includes fluctuations for wide public galaxy surveys like the DES and Euclid, as well as more targeted surveys of various population types, such as those based on redshift, galaxy type, or star formation rates. 

  We have also created a publicly accessible online version of the Precision Calculator that can provide similar estimates for any survey based on its characteristics and those of a specific population being tracked

We demonstrate that weak identification can arise from either a thin or a far-away local extremum, leading to concerns about the reliability of estimates and tests. We present a heuristic approach to gauge the local information available, measuring it by the curvature of the objective function at the estimate. We show that this curvature can be used to evaluate the validity of asymptotic theory, and propose straightforward test metrics to assess weak identification, including a minimum condition and a robustness test. Applying our framework to influential examples, including the Sargent-Wallace model and the analysis of stock prices, we find that key parameters are either poorly or excessively determined. We also explore alternative solutions for strongly identified parameters, including the use of new instruments or alternative estimators. We provide software to access our results and can also offer custom advice on addressing other weakly identified problems.

Combining laser speckle imaging with a Gaussian beam profile, GDSS enables the detection of tumor areas by generating a scanning pattern.  We demonstrated that incorporating machine learning into the GDSS system significantly enhances its performance and efficiency. directly modeled. Our research proposes a new architecture called the reciprocal 
transformer, which redefines the relationship between inputs and outputs by 
exchanging hidden representations and combining them with attention mechanisms. 
We demonstrate that this design reduces the layer number required for self- 
attention modules by approximately 45%. Additionally, the reciprocal 
transformer offers improved training efficiency, achieving a 26% reduction in

at https://github.com/krish310/reciprocal-transformer.  Suppliers and

can be modeled using our reciprocal transformer architecture, but users will 
need to preprocess their data appropriately.  A detailed discussion on how 
to do this effectively is also provided in our study. 

The proposed architecture's performance advantages become more significant when 
working with scarce and high-value data, as noticed in our experiments. 
Moreover, the reciprocal transformer's ability to exchange hidden representations 
between inputs and outputs can be utilized as a structural mixture model, 
which we found to be an useful feature for analyzing the code representations 
of the model. 

We introduced the reciprocal transformer architecture by transforming the 
encoder and decoder modules of a standard transformer model, but we also 
explore alternative designs that involve unifying the encoder and decoder 
modules into a single reciprocal transformer module, which we refer to as 
the N:N reciprocal transformer architecture.

electricity demand, incorporating uncertainty to predict a range of possible

efficient pricing and trading. Consequently, accurate probabilistic load 
forecasts are vital for utilities, renewable energy providers, and aggregators, 
especially with the rise of peer-to-peer trading. 

There are established methods for generating point load forecasts, but 
probabilistic approaches require more consideration. This paper evaluates eight 
different methods for creating probabilistic load forecasts in real-time, using 
data from 15 European utilities. The methods are: a self-adjusting learning 
method; three intra-day persistence approaches; four methods using equivalent 
time-series; and one approach using a grid-based estimation method. The evaluation 
uses mean absolute percentage error (MAPE) and considers factors like season, 
weather, and holidays. The results show that adding utilities' specific 
characteristics can enhance the accuracy of forecasts. Ultimately, a grid-based 
approach proved the most effective for real-time forecasts. 

The study also assesses 16 additional methods with alternative metrics, 
focusing on forecast ranges rather than point values. The evaluation includes 
examining the structure of these forecasts, specifically how they vary over time 
and during different seasons. The results show that adding utilities' specific 
characteristics enhances the accuracy of forecasts. The study further incorporates 
external data to enhance forecasts, exploring the integration of temperature 
forecasts and grid-based approaches. The evaluation of all methods is supported 
by visual analytics, providing a comprehensive evaluation framework that can be 
adapted for future comparisons. 

The study's findings are significant because they provide a comprehensive 
evaluation of probabilistic forecast methods using utility data. The evaluation 
provides a framework and set of best practices for evaluating and comparing 
probabilistic forecasting methods. The code and data used for the evaluation 
are openly available, enabling the comparison to be replicated and expanded 
upon. 

The study's results have practical implications for utilities, renewable energy 
providers, and aggregators, highlighting the importance of utilizing more 
advanced probabilistic forecasting methods to enhance trading strategies and 
efficiency in power markets. The evaluation demonstrates the ability of peer-to-peer 
trading to benefit from accurate probabilistic forecasts, and the potential of 
utilizing external data to enhance forecasts. 

The study's most notable contribution is the comparison of multiple advanced 
probabilistic forecasting methods using utility data, providing a comprehensive 
evaluation framework that can be adapted for future comparisons. The

submmWave technology will likely be the backbone of future wideband wireless communications, enabling numerous frequency-hopping modes for future devices.  To ensure these devices meet conductivity requirements, gold coating is necessitated for optimal conductivity properties.  Therefore, this study is centered on the conductivity characteristics of gold coatings on pc-board substrates, particularly focusing on conductors utilized in mmWave and submmWave applications.  First, a literature review on conductivity theories and their application to gold coatings was conducted.  Next, conductivity tests were carried out on samples with varying thicknesses spanning 0.05 to 1.25 microns, utilizing thick-film gold coatings on commonly used pc-board substrates including FR4, Rogers 4350B, and alumina, among others.  To minimize measurement errors, extensive calibration and multi-batch testing were performed.  Conductivity data was obtained across a frequency range of 50 kHz to 40 GHz, with measurements taken from 8 to 50 times, yielding precise results.  Results showed that conductivity values reach maximum at zero frequency and decrease across the measured frequency range, with a strong frequency dependence noted in thick coatings, whereas the decrease is more pronounced in thinner coatings.  Forming a contrast to this frequency dependence, the alumina samples exhibited the weakest frequency dependence due to their minimal solderability issues.  To address the need for device manufacturers to select the optimal gold coating thickness based on frequency, a simplified thickness selection chart was provided, taking into consideration the diverse applications of mmWave and submmWave devices. This research expands that framework to a broader set of $q$-ary codes. We establish the term '($n,K)$-type ensemble' as a more general expression, referring to an ensemble of code words with predefined indices $n$ and $K$, fitting within the structure of a $q$-ary code that operates on $n$ digits. We also identify the term 'near-perfect' as an attribute of a code's ensemble rather than the ensemble itself. We then prove that a near-perfect code is characterized by an ensemble where the majority of type subsets have the same number of words, and these subsets form a specific structure. We also demonstrate that this condition is also a requirement for a code to have identities. We then examine the relationship between these two properties, identifying that a code with identities is a type of near-perfect code, but the converse is not necessarily true. We then establish an algorithm for calculating the number of words in a near-perfect code's ensemble, and apply this to determine the growth rate of a specific series of near-perfect codes with identities. We also introduce the concept of a code's ensemble having'minimal type complexity', and prove that this is a necessary condition for the ensemble to have the fewest possible number of code words. We then examine the implications of this property on the list decoding problem, and propose an improved bound for the list complexity of code words in an ensemble with minimal type complexity. We also provide an example of a binary Hamming code meeting this condition, and discuss the applicability of this property to other types of codes. We then propose an extension of this framework to combinatorial ensemble theory, and outline potential research directions in this area. We also provide an extension of the Baer-Green lemma for combinatorial ensembles, and propose an explanation for the phenomenon of large minimum distances in certain near-perfect codes. We also examine possible connections between this research and other areas in coding theory, and discuss open questions in this area. We also provide supplementary code for reproducing the main results of this research.

This paper explores the application of control theory to the monsoon system, utilizing a simplified mathematical model that incorporates factors influencing wind and oscillations, as well as a theoretical approach to designing feedback controls for the system. alternative to conventional lithium-ion batteries which are prone to explosions 
and can catch fire. Studies have shown positive results with aluminiumorganic 
cells regarding charge-discharge cycles, energy density and overall safety. 
Notably, aluminium as an anode offers excellent mechanical strength and is nearly 
unlimited in supply, whereas the organic compound in the cathode provides high 
voltage and excellent energy storage. This study focuses on replacing the costly 
sulfur-containing cathode compound with a more affordable and readily available 
phosphorus-containing compound, aiming to enhance the battery's performance. 
Experiments involved synthesizing two different cathode compounds based on 
phosphorus and carbon, along with the aluminiumorganic cell prototype. 
Electrochemical characterization revealed that the two different compounds result in 
similar charge-discharge cycles; however, the phosphorus-containing compound based 
on oxalamic acid delivers a higher operating voltage of up to 2.7 volts, 
comparatively to 2.5 volts of the other compound based on tetrachlorophosphorus 
pentoxide, thus indicating the potential of the oxalamic acid compound for 
improved energy storage. Moreover, the two compounds demonstrated excellent cycle 
stability with a 93 and 90 percent retention of initial capacity for the oxalamic 
acid and tetrachlorophosphorus pentoxide compounds, respectively. 
Accompanying the findings are scanning electron microscopy images and the 
associated potentiostatic tests, along with theoretical calculations of the band 
structures of the two compounds, all contributing to a deeper understanding of 
the aluminiumorganic cell's performance.  Overall, this study introduces a more 
affordable and readily available phosphorus-containing compound as a viable 
alternative to the expensive sulfur-containing compound in aluminiumorganic 
batteries, thus making them more cost-competitive with traditional lithium-ion 
batteries.

cell utilizing the phosphorus-containing compound based on oxalamic acid, 
demonstrating its potential for enhanced energy storage with a maximum operating 
voltage of up to 2.7 volts, along with outstanding cycle stability with 93% 
capacity retention after 800 cycles, making it a promising candidate for 
large-scale energy storage applications in power electronics, electric vehicles 
and grid-scale energy storage systems. 
 
The research also highlights the benefits of utilizing the oxalamic acid compound

Despite their benefits, contact tracing apps have raised users' privacy concerns, prompting analyses of potential data breaches. In response to such analyses, some contact tracing systems have adapted to address users' privacy issues. In contrast to traditional approaches that involve central data collection, these systems leverage device-based strategies, often relying on cryptographic techniques to minimize data exchange. While these contact tracing systems have been analyzed from a security and privacy perspective, there has been little exploration of their functional aspects. A key aspect of this model involves defining the Payoff Matrix for contacts that do not transmit the virus, in order to quantify the benefits of cooperation between users. Optical coherence tomography (OCT) and OCTA, particularly when used with enhanced depth imaging and scanning depths of over 300 microns, have shown strong potential for visualizing and assessing the blood vessels in CNV. 

However, the development of an automated system for detecting and classifying CNV from OCTA images has been hindered by several factors including variations in image quality, the presence of ocular media opacities, the presence of retinal drusen, the presence of red and yellow echoes from the RPE and choroid, and the presence of fading echoes from the distal interface. 

The recent introduction of advanced algorithms for processing OCTA images holds great promise for detecting and masking such artifacts, thereby potentially enhancing the performance of a CNV detection and classification system. 

In this research, we propose a method for processing OCTA images that uses a comprehensive approach combining both global and local analyses to identify artifacts in the images, with a specific focus on enhancing the background subtraction of the OCTA images. 

We tested this proposal using a subset of the data from the AMD OCTA study group, with the results showing a significant improvement in both detection and classification

Since DM interacts with ordinary matter only through gravitational forces, it continues to obscure BHs, even after they have merged with other objects.  This provides us with a motive to investigate the impact of a surrounding DM halo on the gravitational wave signals produced by such BHs, particularly when they merge.  We (for the most part) ignore the influence of self-interacting DM on these signals.  Utilizing an advanced astrophysical simulation, we examined the characteristics of merging BHs within various types of DM halos, which were in turn simulated using the collisionless approximation.  We discovered that the effect of a surrounding halo primarily becomes noticeable at distances closer than ten times the BH's own radius.  This effect varies depending on the mass of the BH and whether it resides at the center of a galaxy or not.  We found that the amplitude of the gravitational wave signals produced by such mergers is reduced by roughly one part in a million due to the presence of the halo, which creates an asymmetry in the merger event.  However, this effect is essentially negligible as compared to other sources of noise in the LIGO detectors.  We also analyzed how the presence of a halo influences the spectral characteristics of the gravitational wave signals, but we were unable to discern any notable features from the data.  On the other hand, we found that the effect of a surrounding halo on the localization of gravitational wave sources through the use of electromagnetic radiation is more significant, but it is still modest, falling short of providing any meaningful insight into the mass-to-light ratio of those sources. approach, particularly its ability to surpass the average performance
of a group of individuals. We refer to these beneficiaries as
"grandchildren." They may access the distilled knowledge gained
from a previous round of superdemocratic deliberation among their
"parents," who comprise the initial group of individuals. This
distilled knowledge takes the form of a simplified and refined
set of options, which the grandchildren can use to make informed
decisions in subsequent rounds of superdemocratic decision-making.
We demonstrate that the grandchildren's performance is akin to
that of a learner who is exposed to the outcomes of a teacher who
isdrawing from a stratified sample of the original set of options.
This results in the grandchildren's performance converging to a
limit that is an average of the performance of the parents, thus
providing the grandchildren with a way to successfully replicate
and improve upon the average performance of previous generations. 
We also explore more complex scenarios in which the parents' set 
of options is not known, as well as scenarios in which the strategic 
behavior of the parents is considered, essentially their ability 
to manipulate the knowledge gained by their grandchildren in order 
to achieve their own desired outcomes. 
Ultimately, this chapter shows that superdemocracy's ability 
to benefit multiple generations provides a way to successfully 
handle situations characterized by a lack of knowledge or strategic 
behavior. 
We have designed and tested a protocol that is based on this 
theory and is capable of being implemented using a variety 
of superdemocratic decision-making methods, including those 
that prioritize fairness and security.

under certain conditions and is capable of generating 
actionable recommendations in real-world scenarios, as 
demonstrated through our own practical applications 
of this protocol.

our results to a group of experts in the field, who 
provided us with their thoughts and feedback.

will have a significant impact on the development 
of strategies that are capable of being implemented 
by multiple generations of individuals working 
together, as well as the development of techniques 
that are capable of handling strategic behavior

One crucial aspect involves accurately determining the size of objects in images, which we explore through the lens of one specific class of animals - sharks. In real-world scenarios, sharks occupy a significant portion of ocean surfaces and have distinct physical features that make them amenable to size estimation. However, estimating the size of sharks in ocean environments presents a more complex problem due to the lack of size information in images and the difficulty of collecting large, diverse datasets. In our research, we address this issue by introducing a novel approach called Relative Size Transfer, which enables the prediction of object sizes in new environments from those in well-annotated settings, given only a small set of images with size information and a comprehensive database of object annotations. Our method involves several key components, including a static part that uses a regression module to predict sizes in new environments based on similar-looking images, a dynamic part that incorporates additional visual information to make more accurate predictions over time, and a unidirectional transfer mechanism that allows for the exchange of size information between environments. Through extensive experiments and a thorough analysis of our results, we demonstrate the significant improvements achieved by our proposed approach over existing methods in various datasets, including the Shark Size Estimation Dataset introduced in this paper. Our study provides valuable insights into one of the key components of the 3D object detection pipeline, sheds light on the challenging problem of size estimation for objects with consistent but not identical appearances, and paves the way for future research in this area. lead halide perovskite material has been consistently demonstrated, yet the underlying reason for this phenomenon remains subject to debate.  Our investigation employs both photoluminescence and time-resolved photoluminescence spectroscopies to examine the dynamic process occurring in the material after a photoluminescence event.  We propose that the long-lived photoluminescence is not solely the result of a reduced recombination rate, but rather is influenced by the perovskite's charge carrier dynamics, which are determined by their mobility and concentration.  Our findings indicate that the long-lived photoluminescence is actually an indication of the perovskite's ambipolar properties, which are not affected by an applied electric field.  We observe that the perovskite's charge carrier mobility can be increased while its ambipolar nature persists, offering potential advantages for the development of optical communications using the perovskite material.  Our study provides a more comprehensive understanding of the perovskite's photophysics, which is critical for the optimization of the material for photonic applications. whether a student learns a programming language in the context of a specific subject like mathematics or general-purpose context. This study like its predecessor assessed both approaches but focused on problem-solving using a specific method. High school students solved algebraic puzzles using logic and a programming language to solve them. The key difference was whether students used a general-purpose language or one specifically designed for logical operations. The results showed that the choice of programming language didn't affect the students' ability to solve the puzzles. However, further analysis revealed that when the puzzles required a sequence of steps to arrive at the solution, the choice of programming language became a factor. In such cases, students who used the general-purpose language performed better. In contrast, when the puzzles could be solved with a single step, there was no significant difference. Additionally, the way students used the programming language seemed to depend on its design, influencing their problem-solving strategies. In such cases, the usual advantages of general-purpose languages held an advantage over specialized ones. This study's outcome was counter to our initial hypotheses, underscoring the significance of programming language on problem-solving methods. It also highlights the importance of further exploring this phenomenon, likely to yield insights that could enhance both the teaching of programming and the development of programming languages. 

  This research is an outgrowth of a project where students learned a programming language within the context of an algebra course. The original study assessed two approaches to teaching this course, using a general-purpose language versus one specifically designed for logical operations. The results showed no significant difference in the students' ability to solve the puzzles, leading us to hypothesize that either type of language would be sufficient. However, some students expressed a preference for the general-purpose language due to its broader applicability and greater ease of use. In contrast, the specialized language was easier to read and understand. In the follow-up study, we kept the same variables but included additional puzzles of a different nature. The results confirmed our initial finding, showing no significant difference in the students' ability to solve the new puzzles.

Given their enhanced sensitivity and expanded sky coverage, these experiments are capable of detecting the intrinsic anisotropy of CMB maps on a universal scale of one minute.  However, CMB maps also contain larger structures that arise from the movement of the observer and contribute to the anisotropy.  The line-of-sight is not continuously unobstructed, as there are intervening galaxies that absorb CMB photons, creating structures that are both horizontally extended and vary in depth.  These structures, which extend over an incredibly large range of depths, pose a major challenge to analyzing CMB data.  The depth of these structures is not just randomly distributed but instead correlates with the horizontal extent due to the movement of the observer, creating a statistical link between their sizes and the rate at which anisotropies change.  This paper delves into an approach where the anisotropy of CMB maps is viewed through a convolution lens, leveraging the movement of the observer to understand the cross-correlation of CMB maps with other celestial bodies, and explores the possibility of recovering the anisotropy of CMB maps through deconvolution.   We propose a novel task, Named Entity Translation, which involves translating named entities from one language to another while maintaining their original context. This task becomes particularly relevant when considering the disparity between formal and informal language in Turkish. 

  For instance, the name "Twitter" can be translated from English to Turkish as both "Twitter" and "Twiter", yet the context in which each appears differs significantly.   We developed a technique that allows entities to be translated while taking into account their surrounding context, which in turn allows us to leverage this method for the Named Entity Translation task. 

  We created a dataset consisting of 5 languages and over 21,000 entities, which we utilized to demonstrate that context is indeed an essential factor in entity translation. 

  We observed that employing context aids in overcoming translation ambiguities, which in turn leads to enhanced entity translation accuracy. 

  We implemented three different techniques, which we discovered excelled in handling context and ambiguity simultaneously, resulting in improved entity translation accuracy. 

  We demonstrated that our approach excelled in NMT, substantially outperforming the standard approach by achieving an F1 score of 0.65 in our primary dataset and 0.46 in the CoNLL2002 dataset for Named Entity Recognition. 

  We also found that our method proved particularly beneficial for low-resource languages, enhancing entity translation accuracy in Turkish by 11% in comparison to the standard approach.

's crucial for startups 
working with government agencies to have a clear understanding of the Intellectual 
Property (IP) strategies employed by these agencies. This survey aims to gather 
opinions from German startups on their experiences and perceptions of IP policies 
within government agencies, with a focus on R&D collaborations. The results reveal 
key insights: startups generally believe agencies' IP strategies are unclear, with 
consequences including delayed project developments, increased costs, and lost 
business opportunities. Many startups have adapted IP policies from a previous 
study, 
with additional key findings: they tend to choose flexible IP strategies over 
rigid ones and often select strategies based on collaboration areas and partner 
types. Collaborations with public research institutions lead startups to adopt 
more flexible IP strategies, whereas collaborations with universities and 
hospitals induce a preference for more rigid strategies. Furthermore, startups 
tend to pick IP strategies that align with those of their primary collaboration 
partner. Measures to enhance IP transparency and efficiency, such as providing 
IP guidelines at the outset of projects, are also identified through the data, 
alongside several potential areas for future research. This study's findings can 
serve as a call to action for German government agencies to revise their IP 
policies in order to create more favorable conditions for startups and technology 
transfer. 

Keywords: 
Intellectual Property, R&D collaborations, government agencies, startup firms, 
technology transfer, cooperative strategies.

from neutral atoms inside plasma volumes that are inaccessible to in-situ measurements plays a crucial role in understanding plasma-wall interactions during tokamak access.  As these measurements are subject to interference from multiple sources of Doppler broadened neutral atomic D-alpha lines, it is essential to identify and filter out signals originating from plasma rather than wall sources.  We propose a new method for accomplishing this, utilizing measurements of D-alpha line widths in combination with spatial profiles, to differentiate between the spectra produced by the plasma and wall sources.  We demonstrate this technique's effectiveness using two D-alpha filters located at different distances from the tokamak's wall, where one is influenced primarily by plasma volumes and the other by much smaller wall-facing plasma interfaces.  We found that the method successfully discriminates between the two sources of D-alpha emission, confirming that broad D-alpha lines with enhanced intensities originate from small, inaccessible plasma interfaces with the wall.  We also found that D-alpha line widths return to their normal widths after neutralizing the wall with a large dose of neutrons, indicating that wide D-alpha lines are a neutron wall-induced phenomenon.  We propose that this D-alpha filter technique could be expanded across the entire D-alpha line spectrum to gain more in-depth information about inaccessible plasma interfaces with the wall, utilizing all available optical diagnostic data.  We demonstrate that this method can be modelled with high accuracy using neutral atom transport calculations, which utilize cross-sections for neutral atomic interactions with both plasma and wall sources, providing a powerful tool to investigate these inaccessible plasma interfaces. As a related concept, additive neural networks have emerged with their own benefits, guaranteeing explanatory models and being resistant to manipulation.  Additive models essentially take the form of decision trees, however, they can't handle complex data on their own and typically require the incorporation of interaction terms.  The process of identifying these terms is usually done through exhaustive search methods that are either impractical due to their high computational cost or ineffective because they don't consider neural network representations.  We address this challenge by developing a method that makes use of the representation already learned by the neural network, allowing us to find a subset of interaction terms that have the greatest impact on the model's performance.  This method can be applied to any neural network-based additive model and has a relatively low computational cost, making it suitable for extensive search over a range of candidate terms.  We demonstrate the effectiveness of our method through a series of experiments conducted across multiple datasets and applications. As non-uniform magnetic fields are applied, the pattern of rotation in the map shifts, eventually reaching a steady-state configuration. The extent of this shift is found to be proportional to the gradient of the magnetic field. Nonetheless, a notable aspect in the development of these agents has gone largely unreported - the process of selecting episode lengths for training.  Our research uncovers the crucial role episode length plays in the performance of these agents, as it significantly impacts their overall skill level. Combining the 2.5 post-Newtonian expansion with a leading order post-Newtonian hydrodynamic description can model the merger process for many types of objects.  However, the combination of these expansions results in an overly complex, solvable but only approximate description of the merger.  Typically, this is used to make predictions about gravitational waves emitted during the merger.  In this study, we determine how accurately these predictions hold compared to a direct numerical solution of the Einstein field equations.  We compare both the 2.5 post-Newtonian expansion and a hydrodynamic description to a numerical solution for binary black hole mergers of intermediate mass ratios.  We find that the amplitude, phase, and spectrum of the gravitational waves match the predictions to within a part in ten thousand, however the predictions fail to account for how the gravitational waves are bent around the black holes.  We also find that the post-Newtonian expansion and the hydrodynamic description are both equally accurate, showing that the hydrodynamic description can model the merger process even when the objects' surfaces are not distorted.  We attribute the accuracy of the predictions to the symmetry of the merger and hypothesize that more asymmetric mergers may be modeled less accurately.  We also find that increasing the objects' spins has very little effect on the gravitational waves, which conflicts with previous studies that found a stronger relationship, often due to them not accounting for the effects of spin on the gravitational wave detector.  Ultimately, this provides a more reliable set of equations for predicting the gravitational waves emitted during the merger and highlights the limitations of these predictions, which will be marginally accurate at best for the next generation of gravitational wave detectors. as TQA and TITAN, are not sufficient to train models that can answer arbitrary natural language questions because they are curated with additional constraints.  For example, they require the questions to be related to a specific section of text.  To improve question answering on such constraints, researchers have been answering questions based on the presence or absence of specific words or phrases in the text.  However, questions posed in everyday life are often not as constrained as this.  To address this issue, we introduced a dataset called QASPER, which includes a variety of boolean labels for sentences generated by TQA models.  We discovered that constraints posed by true or false labels can be very complex and comprise over 150 different kinds of relations.  Additionally, we found that simply determining the presence or absence of words or phrases is not sufficient to explain the labels and that more sophisticated patterns are necessary, such as syntactic and semantic relationships, which involve entities, relations, and attributes.  To further illustrate the intricacy of these patterns, we developed a method to visualize the distributions of labels within each instance of the dataset and found that the patterns that underlie the labels are highly instance-specific, which poses a challenge for developing generalizable theories to explain the labels and raises questions about how they could be learned in an instance-specific manner.

  To tackle this problem, we proposed another approach that focuses on the question generator rather than the relation between the question and the text, which involves training a model to generate questions that are capable of detecting complex patterns in the text.  We demonstrated that this approach leads to significant improvements in the overall accuracy of the model and that the questions generated in this manner are not only more accurate but also more concise and more natural-sounding, which indicates that they could be more suitable for tasks such as question-answering and data augmentation.  We also discovered that these questions are capable of detecting not only entities, relations, and attributes but also aspects that are implicit in the text, which further suggests that they could be more effective at inferring implicit evidence and combining explicit evidence with additional common-sense knowledge.  We evaluated our approach using the QASPER dataset, which comprises 280k training examples, 2k validation examples, and 10k testing examples, and found that it achieves state-of-the-art performance compared to other question-answering models, which includes the use of explicit constraints, entity-based approaches, and document-level attention, as well as the application of additional aids such as auxiliary tasks and semantic role labeling

This model incorporates a general dynamic factor model and utilizes a specific type of distribution, namely the multivariate normal, to facilitate the accommodation of negative values and heavy-tailed phenomena.  To estimate and conduct inference, we have developed a method that builds upon the work of several leading researchers in the field, specifically for the case of subgaussian variables.  Although the method is robust for variables with heavier tails, it lacks formal theoretical justification in these instances.  To address this limitation, we estimate the model using two alternative methods - the conditional mean - and the conditional median - and demonstrate that these estimators provide reliable results, even in the presence of variables with heavier outer tails.  To address issues related to time variation, we have developed a new method, specifically the wild kernel estimator, which enables us to accurately estimate the parameters of the model.  To evaluate the model's performance, we utilize several common metrics, including the BIC information criterion and lagged covariance estimates.  To investigate the model's applicability, we estimate the time-varying component for multiple variables, specifically stock prices, trading volumes and foreign exchange rates, throughout the year 2020, a period marked by the COVID-19 pandemic, and assess the model's performance using data from the New York Stock Exchange.  To examine the model's ability to forecast variables with heavy tails, we estimate the distribution of the forecast errors for multiple variables, including Apple Inc. stock prices and trading volumes, and conduct surveys among finance experts to gather qualitative insights.  Finally, we estimate the model for multiple variables, including the S&P 500 stock price index and the European Union export price index, and analyze the co-movements of the variables using data from the New York Stock Exchange, the European Union export price index, the Japanese stock market, and the Australian stock market.

in a machine learning system by employing human labelers to mark a limited number of data points for classification.  The remaining unlabelled data is then used to train a classifier using standard, non-active methods.  An alternative known as self-labeling involves using the pre-trained classifier to generate its own labels for a subset of unlabelled data, effectively creating pseudo-labels. The goal of this research is to investigate whether self-labeling can be an effective active learning method by designating a small set of labelled data, then gradually increasing the number of self-labeled data points over multiple iterations.  We evaluate self-labeling by comparing it to conventional active learning methods on four image classification datasets.  Our results demonstrate that self-labeling yields superior classification accuracy across the board,  indicating that the strategy has significant advantages as a machine learning method.  We further analyze the relationship between the number of data points selected for self-labelling at each iteration and the overall performance of the classifier,  finding that a more nuanced approach can be used to guide the selection process by utilising the confidence levels of the pre-trained classifier in conjunction with metrics such as the density of labelled data points.  We conclude that self-labeling presents a novel, compelling solution to the challenge of efficiently scaling machine learning in relation to large datasets and limited labelled data. " Exoplanet Transit List" and "Exoplanet Ephemerides" are analyzed in order to identify patterns of co-orbital exoplanets.  A statistical analysis was performed to determine the occurrence of co-orbital pairs, and the results revealed a higher than expected number of co-orbital pairs, with a margin of error less than 0.01, indicating that co-orbital exoplanets are not uncommon.  Additionally, a preference was observed for the mass ratio of co-orbital exoplanets to be around 2.5 or greater, with a preferred orientation of their orbits and a tendency for their primary stars to be in the G, K, or M spectral categories.  It was also found that primary stars with low masses tend to host multiple co-orbital exoplanets, while primary stars with high masses typically only host one co-orbital exoplanet.  The distribution of semi-major axes for co-orbital exoplanets tends to follow a logarithmic pattern, and the majority of co-orbital exoplanets are found in planetary systems that also contain small, tightly bound objects known as exoplanet companions.  The findings from this study may be the result of selection bias, sample bias, or a genuine phenomenon, and the latter possibility could be the consequence of a primary star's angular momentum being reduced due to the transfer of mass from a companion object in a close orbit.  The results from this analysis are meant to be a preliminary step in investigating the dynamics of co-orbital exoplanets and their relationships with the planetary systems in which they are found.  The detection rate of co-orbital exoplanets can be enhanced through the use of highly precise radial velocity measurements, and the technique of combining data from multiple sources can also be employed to improve the accuracy of the calculations. This filter causes the transfer of energy from the initial meridional flow to the zonal flow, following the requirements of the geostrophic filter. We are then able to determine the linear response of the zonal flow to an arbitrary initial meridional flow, which we find takes the form of a superposition of modes determined by the ratio of the rotation rate to the frequency of each mode. We confirm our results with numerical simulations, which demonstrate the accuracy of our response theory. We also examine the impact of increasing rotation rates on the transfer of energy from the meridional flow to the zonal flow, which shows the rotation rate must exceed a certain threshold before the transfer occurs, a phenomenon we attribute to the breakdown of the geostrophic filter. We further observe that this transfer process becomes more efficient as the rotation rate increases, provided the rotation rate exceeds this threshold. We also uncover the emergence of Rossby waves in our response theory, which we are able to include in our simplified one-dimensional problem. We identify a specific subgroup within the symmetric group Sn, known as the wreath-like subgroup, that exhibits the odd class pair property.  The wreath-like subgroup can be thought of as a twisted version of the subgroup generated by the n-cycles in Sn.  By demonstrating that the wreath-like subgroup possesses the odd class pair property, we are able to generalize this property to other groups that contain this subgroup as a normal subset.  This leads to an investigation of the group Wn x Fi, where Fi represents the simple subgroups within the alternating group An.  The odd class pair property is exhibited by the group Wn, but not seen in the groups W2k or Kn, where k is greater than 1. To effectively operate in coexistence mode, satellite transmitters must accurately detect the signals from other satellites and adjust their modulation schemes accordingly. However, the presence of cross-talk from adjacent transmitters can cause detection errors, leading to inappropriate modulation scheme choices and reducing the effective capacity of the satellite network.

A new detector is proposed that takes into account the cross-talk from adjacent transmitters and employs a probability density function (PDF) developed using information from the transmitter and receiver ends. The proposed detector outperforms the conventional decision directive detector in simulations of real-world applications. 

Furthermore, the PDF is utilized to create a new detection metric, known as the minimum error hamming distance, which outperforms the conventional decision directive detector in simulations of scenarios where there is no cross-talk or the cross-talk does not affect the detection, as well as in scenarios where there is severe cross-talk.

is now a well-known challenge in the 
field of computer vision, particularly in the context of object detection. 
COD demands a model not only to identify objects but also to determine which 
objects are intentionally obscured from view. 
Recent COD studies have achieved notable success thanks to the advancement of 
deep learning models, particularly those incorporating boundary information, 
yet these studies have thus far been limited to detecting naturally occurring 
camouflaged objects on specific datasets, such as the COD2019 and COD2020 
benchmark datasets. 
Conversely, the task of detecting artificially created codewords, as seen in 
the Codeword Completion (CC) dataset, proves far more challenging. 
Existing CC detection models fail to perform well on difficult samples 
characterized by thin boundaries, low activation values in feature maps, 
difficult occlusion conditions, and poor codeword designs. 
To address these shortfalls, we have introduced a new COD dataset called COD5k, 
featuring 5020 annotated images containing artificially created codewords, 
together with an in-depth analysis of five challenging scenarios commonly found 
in COD5k. 
To bridge the gap between codeword detection on the COD5k dataset and natural 
object detection, we have designed a new decoder module and overall network 
architecture called the Codeword-Aware Object Detection (CodAwOD) model, 
utilizing a boundary-featured encoder and a decoupled decoder mechanism to 
synergistically explore object boundaries and encode codewords. 
By thoroughly evaluating our CodAwOD model on the COD5k dataset, it has been 
found to achieve state-of-the-art performance compared to other codeword detection 
models, while also exhibiting comparable performance to natural object detection 
models on difficult samples. 
Furthermore, a comprehensive study was conducted to analyze the performance of 
CodAwOD on the COD2019 and COD2020 benchmark datasets, resulting in the model 
achieving state-of-the-art performance, as well as an in-depth analysis of the 
source code, dataset, and experimental setup being made freely available at 
the CodAwOD GitHub repository.  CodAwOD has also been found to be robust in 
multi-object scenario cases and using CodAwOD on the COD2019 dataset after 
introducing artificial codewords for an object results in the model being able 
to detect the additional codewords.  CodAwOD has the potential to be a top 
contender for future COD benchmark datasets.
